Academic Impact and the COVID-19 Pandemic

• As we are all aware, the COVID-19 pandemic has upended the lives of people both in the
 US and worldwide.
• The pandemic has dramatically impacted the physical, emotional, a financial status of
 people both in the US and worldwide.
• Students did not avoid the impact of the pandemic as their education changed
 dramatically in early 2020 and those changes reverberated into 2021.
• From the first stages of the pandemic, there was a desire to understand the academic
 impact of the pandemic (comprising all the myriad ways the pandemic changed
 education) on students.
• Like most aspects of life, student academic testing was severely disrupted during the first
 stages of the pandemic leaving little comprehensive data on student attainment
• As the pandemic stretched into the 2020-2021 school year, data from interim assessment
 providers became available to help begin to assess the academic impact of the pandemic
 on students.

What does COVID-19 academic impact mean?

• Several terms have been used to discuss pandemic related
 academic impact including Learning Loss, Unfinished Learning,
 and COVID-slide
• The terminology used is contentious.
• If, in fact, the pandemic has had a negative impact, overall, on
 the academic attainment of students, whether the lower
 attainment is due to learning loss (skill atrophy), unfinished
 learning, or some combination is unknown.
• We use the terms interchangeably without ascribing the
 underlying mechanism of lower attainment.

What do we mean by “Learning Loss”

 • Understanding pandemic related
 academic impact/learning loss requires a
 counter-factual: Where would the
 student/group/system be if the pandemic
 hadn’t happened.
 • We can’t observe the counterfactual.
 • Using historical data, we can attempt to
 model the counterfactual.
 • For example, assuming the student would
 have demonstrated typical pre-COVID
 academic growth, how far behind (ahead)
 is the student?

What do we mean by “Learning Loss”

 • A decrease in student growth leads to
 a decrease in attainment.
 • Similarly, lower attainment implies
 that the growth for the student was
 lower.
 • Deviation from historically typical
 growth can be used to quantify the
 academic impact of the pandemic.

Renaissance STAR Assessments and Student Growth
• Since 2010, Renaissance Learning has been calculating student growth
 percentiles (SGPs) for students on their STAR mathematics, reading, and early
 literacy assessments.
• The RLI STAR student growth percentiles differ slightly from those used as part
 of state assessments:
 • STAR assessments are administered through the year in Fall (August to November),
 Winter (December to March) and Spring (April to June) assessment windows.
 • Growth is calculated across several permutations of the assessment windows: Fall-to-
 Fall, Fall-to-Winter, Fall-to-Spring, Winter-to-Spring, Spring-to-Spring, Spring-to-Fall.
 • Students do not take the assessments on the same date, so quantile regression
 modelling takes account of:
 • Up to two prior achievement scores
 • Time during the window when test is taken (i.e., number of days since beginning of window)
 • Time-lag to the prior test (i.e., number of days to the first prior test)
 • See this report for more details.

Renaissance STAR Assessments and Student Growth

• STAR SGPs grew out of Renaissance Learning’s efforts to create historical growth
 norms using gain scores from their vertical scale.
• SGPs calculated using gain scores as the dependent variable are equivalent to SGPs
 calculated using the most recent score as the dependent variable.
• Renaissance Learning generates SGPs in real-time for students using their cloud-
 based analytics platform and the SGP package based upon the R software
 environment (Betebenner, Van Iwaarden, Domingue, and Shang, 2021).
• Generating SGPs in real-time requires pre-existing growth norms (i.e., coefficient
 matrices) to be used.
• At present, coefficient matrices utilized to calculate SGPs for STAR assessments are
 based upon 2015-16, 2016-17, and 2017-18 STAR results and utilize between
 500,000–and 1,000,000 students in each grade and content area.

SGP interpretation
• For the entire norm group of students on which the coefficient matrices (growth
 norms) are derived:
 • SGPs have mean/median of 50
 • SGPs are uncorrelated with prior (initial) achievement.
• For SGPs calculated using later cohorts of students:
 • Mean/median SGPs for subgroups (e.g., demographic subgroups, schools, districts) will
 usually differ from 50. That is, it is not uncommon to see growth gaps.
 • Mean SGP differences between groups of 5 correspond to an effect size of 0.18.
• Covid related academic impact for groups can be determined by calculating:
 Mean SGPgroup, pre-Covid – Mean SGPgroup, Covid
• That is, how much has growth (i.e. learning) slowed down due to COVID.
• My co-presenters will be providing numerous results.

SGP and the assessment of academic impact

• Historically, the least utilized SGPs calculated by STAR was
 probably Fall-to-Fall growth.
• With a pandemic striking the world in the spring, Fall-to-Fall
 growth took on particular relevance.
• Fall 2019 to Fall 2020 SGPs allowed Renaissance to evaluate
 academic impact due to COVID.
• Fall 2020 to Winter 2021 and Winter 2021 to Spring 2021 SGPs
 allow Renaissance to evaluate both impact and potentially initial
 recovery.

Four types of recovery

• Borrowing terminology from economics,
 STAR SGPs will broadly allow stakeholders
 to plan for and evaluate:
 • V-shaped recovery -- Immediate snap-back to
 non-pandemic trajectory
 • U-shaped recovery – More gradual move back
 toward non-pandemic trajectory
 • L-shaped recovery – Not a recovery but not
 falling further behind.
 • Academic downward spiral – Continue to fall
 further and further behind.

• At a system level, beware the K-shaped
 recovery where high achievers/advantaged
 predominantly experience V- and U-shaped
 recoveries and low achievers/
 disadvantaged don’t recover.

Threats to interpretation

• There are several threats to the validity of STAR interim
 assessment SGP results.
 • It was difficult to distinguish Fall 2020 test takers who took the exam at
 home and took the exam at school.
 • The students for whom we have growth data in 2021 might be different
 than those with growth data in 2020.
 • Students absent from testing in Fall 2020
 • Changing customer base
 • Scale drift would undermine the use of historical growth norms (i.e.,
 baseline SGP coefficient matrices) which presume no scale drift.

Descriptive accountability

Accountability system results can have value without making causal
inferences about school quality, solely from the results of student
achievement measures and demographic characteristics. Treating the
results as descriptive information and for identification of schools that
require more intensive investigation of organizational and
instructional process characteristics are potentially of considerable
value. Rather than using the results of the accountability system as
the sole determiner of sanctions for schools, they could be used to
flag schools that need more intensive investigation to reach sound
conclusions about needed improvements or judgments about quality
 Robert Linn, 2008, p. 21
